name: Freya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a freelance subtitler and game translator, Danish and German into English. A normal day is me in my flat with two screens: on one, a crime series episode, on the other, my subtitle file, and an AI tool drafting lines I then rewrite for timing and tone. A couple of afternoons a month I interpret at video calls for a Danish furniture company. I love making a joke land in another language, and I hate clients who think that takes five minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of your day runs through AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty much all of it now. I've built my own setup: the AI drafts, a second tool checks terms against the show's glossary, and I do the human part, which is rhythm and jokes and swearing that sounds real. It's roughly doubled the episodes I can do in a week. I share the setup with a little group of freelancers I met on a forum, because I'd rather we all keep up than fight over scraps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's fine with me, the tools I've got already help a lot. I'd post in my freelancers' forum that we should stop panicking and start pricing our time properly. And I'd say the bigger fight is streaming platforms paying per minute rates that haven't moved in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau is basically my sweet spot. My setup gives me an edge over people who refused the tools, and nothing comes along to wipe that edge out. I'd still want fairer rates, but my income would feel solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my setup and take on a third regular client, maybe a game studio. I'd help my forum group set up a shared rate card so nobody undercuts. And I'd move my savings from about three months to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly a bit pleased. It's the version where my early bet pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your group would struggle even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, who only does literary translation and refuses the tools on principle. He's brilliant, but he's slow, and publishers pay by the book. Even in a quiet AI world, Jonas (a literary translator in my group) earns less than me for better work, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the extra time on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More games, because that's where the fun writing is. A fantasy game might have a hundred thousand words of dialogue, and half of it is wizards being sarcastic. I'd also take one weekend a month off, which I haven't done in a year.

say: The tools **already help** a lot, so I'd tell people to stop panicking.
The bigger fight is **streaming rates** that haven't moved in years.
think: A plateau is my **sweet spot**, keeping my edge over people who refused the tools.
My income would feel **solid**, even if rates stay unfair.
do: Take on a **game studio** as a third regular client.
Set up a **shared rate card** with her freelancer forum group.
**Grow savings** from about three months to five.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **pleased**, as her early bet on AI tools pays off.
S0.quote: Even in a quiet AI world, Jonas (a literary translator in my group) earns less than me for better work, and that bothers me.
fieldNote: She is **genuinely secure** here: high output, steady clients and growing savings.
Her **progressive streak** shows as shared rate cards, not protests.
She feels uneasy about **fairness to others**, not about her own income.

steps.text: Add a game studio as a third regular client
Refine the AI subtitle setup with a glossary checker
Draft a shared rate card with the forum group
Build savings from three to five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where translators who learned the tools do fine and the rest get hurt, and that's not fair. I'd post guides for my forum group on how to set up what I've got. I'd also say platforms should share the savings, not pocket them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay for a while, but the floor under me gets lower. If streaming platforms run whole series through AI and only pay for a quick polish, my per-episode rate falls even if I do more episodes. I'd stay busy, but I'd be running faster to earn the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift toward game localisation, where tone and culture matter more and studios still pay for creative work. I'd start a small co-op with three people from the forum, so we can bid for bigger game contracts together. And I'd keep savings at five months, no new spending on gear this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also kind of energised. I like problems I can work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a co-op actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A studio with a big fantasy game won't hire one freelancer for four languages, but they'll hire a co-op. We'd share the AI setup, the glossaries and the contracts. It's the closest thing freelancers get to a union, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay but running faster. Isn't that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If I'm doing twelve episodes a week to earn what eight paid last year, that's burnout, not success. I'd have to watch for that, and so would my group.

say: Translators who **learned the tools** do fine, and the rest get hurt.
Platforms should **share the savings** from AI, not pocket them.
think: My **per-episode rate** falls even as I do more episodes.
I'd stay busy, but I'd be **running faster** to earn the same.
do: **Shift toward game** localisation, where tone and culture still earn more.
**Start a co-op** with three forum freelancers to bid for bigger contracts.
**Hold savings** at five months and skip new gear this year.
feel: **Uneasy but energised**, enjoying a problem she can work on.
S1.quote: If I'm doing twelve episodes a week to earn what eight paid last year, that's burnout, not success.
fieldNote: Her income looks **safe for now**, but she sees the floor dropping.
**Co-op idea** blends her progressive views with a business plan.
Worried about **burnout** more than job loss in this scenario.

steps.text: Move most work toward game localisation contracts
Form a four-person translators' co-op from the forum
Keep five months saved and skip new equipment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need a basic income or something like it, fast, because two years is nothing. I'd be loud about it online, and I'd join whatever campaign was organising. I'd tell people not to blame themselves for not seeing it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my whole setup becomes pointless. I'm the human doing rhythm and jokes, and AGI does rhythm and jokes. Being early with the AI tools buys me maybe a year over everyone else, and then I'm in the same queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use that year to earn as much as I possibly could and save it. I'd look hard at work that's hands-on or face to face, because the robots are three years behind, maybe running language tours for visitors to Copenhagen with my cousin. And I'd join the campaign for an income guarantee, because I'd honestly need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops picturing it, mostly because there's no clever move left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why language tours, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's walking, talking and being a person in a place. My cousin Mette already runs bike tours, and she's said she'd take me on. It's a third of what I earn now, but it's people paying for a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your forum group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that my setup won't save any of us now. Then I'd suggest we pool what we know about other jobs and help each other find something. That's what I'd want someone to do for me.

say: We need a **basic income** or something like it, fast.
People shouldn't **blame themselves** for not seeing it coming.
think: My whole **AI setup** becomes pointless, because AGI does rhythm and jokes too.
Being early buys me **maybe a year** before I'm in the same queue.
do: **Earn and save** as much as possible in the first year.
**Look into running** language tours with her cousin's bike tour business.
**Join the campaign** for a guaranteed income.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a dropping stomach, because no clever move is left.
S2.quote: Being early with the AI tools buys me maybe a year over everyone else, and then I'm in the same queue.
fieldNote: Her adaptability **stops helping** once AGI does her creative part too.
Turns to **face-to-face work**, using the robot delay, at a big pay cut.
Her first instinct is **to warn and help** her forum group.

steps.text: Save as much of the first year's income as possible
Join cousin Mette's tour business leading language tours
Join the campaign for a guaranteed basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a safety net, so let's build one. I'd write posts on what freelancers specifically need, because we always fall through the gaps. And I'd tell younger translators not to start a degree in this now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get three or four good years out of my setup and the co-op. Then I'd need something else by thirty-one or thirty-two. That's actually a decent age to switch, if I start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the co-op hard for two years and save at least a third of what I earn. In year two I'd start a part-time course in something people-facing, probably teaching or speech therapy, which uses what I know about language. And I'd keep pushing the forum group to plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be making lists, not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why speech therapy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always been fascinated by how people make sounds, and it's in a room with a child or a stroke patient. That's thinking work, so AGI touches part of it, but the hands-on part waits for the robots. It feels like language, just with a person attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still recommend translation to anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a career, no. I'd tell my cousin's kid to learn languages for life, not for a job, and that's a sad thing for me to say.

say: **Five years** is enough time to build a proper **safety net** for freelancers.
Young people shouldn't start **translation degrees** now, because the work won't last.
think: I'd get **three or four years** from my setup and the co-op.
Switching careers at **thirty-one** is doable if I start planning now.
do: **Run the co-op** hard for two years and save a third of earnings.
**Start a part-time course** in speech therapy or teaching in year two.
**Keep the forum group** planning their exits together.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, making lists rather than lying awake.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin's kid to learn languages for life, not for a job, and that's a sad thing for me to say.
fieldNote: She **expects to lose** translation work but has time and a clear plan.
**Speech therapy** keeps her close to language and to people.
Her advice to young people shows **how final** she thinks this is.

steps.text: Save a third of co-op earnings for two years
Begin a part-time speech therapy course in year two
Organise exit planning sessions for the forum group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for any translator to be caught out. I'd post a long thread about what to do year by year. I'd also say government should start funding mid-career retraining now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels mostly like opportunity for someone like me. The co-op could grow, and I'd have time to train properly in something new without panic. The risk is that rates drop a lot sooner than 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the co-op to maybe eight people and take on bigger game projects. Around year four I'd start the speech therapy degree part time, funded from the co-op. And I'd keep savings at six months, because freelance rates could fall early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a bit of nervousness about the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rates could drop sooner. What would you watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same thing the streaming platforms did first. When the big game studios ask for AI first draft plus review on everything, I'd start the speech therapy degree that same autumn. I wouldn't wait for 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. I'd still want to travel and maybe live in Copenhagen for a year. Ten years is long enough that I wouldn't put my life on hold.

say: With **ten years**, no translator has an excuse to be caught out.
Government should **fund retraining** for mid-career workers now.
think: Ten years mostly means **opportunity** for someone like me.
The real risk is **rates dropping** well before 2036.
do: **Grow the co-op** to about eight people with bigger game projects.
**Start a speech therapy** degree part time around year four.
**Keep six months** saved in case rates fall early.
feel: **Mostly hopeful**, with some nerves about timing.
S4.quote: When the big game studios ask for AI first draft plus review on everything, I'd start the speech therapy degree that same autumn.
fieldNote: She knows **translation ends** for her, but feels in control of the exit.
Has a **clear trigger** for starting her retraining.
Keeps **life plans** like travel going, unlike more anxious peers.

steps.text: Grow the translators' co-op to about eight members
Enrol part time in a speech therapy degree around year four
Hold six months of expenses in savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. My whole advantage is being quick with the tools, and that's worth nothing if the tools do everything in two years. What would help is an income guarantee for the gap, and free, paid retraining for people moving into face-to-face work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about freelancers specifically. We've got no employer, no redundancy pay and no HR to tell us what's coming. When a client stops emailing a freelancer, nobody says goodbye.

headlineQuote: When a client stops emailing a freelancer, nobody says goodbye.
portrait: A **27-year-old freelance** subtitler and game translator working from Danish and German into English.
Uses **AI tools daily** in a setup she built and shares with other freelancers.
**Calm to uneasy** in milder pictures, then alarmed when AGI makes her edge worthless.
Turns to **co-ops and campaigns**, mixing progressive views with practical business plans.
Plans an **exit into speech therapy** or face-to-face work as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her advantage with the tools vanishes in two years.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee** to cover the gap between careers.
**Paid retraining** for moving into face-to-face work.
